newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japanese stocks gather forces for further ascent.
newsitem.headline: Japanese stocks gather forces for further ascent.

text.p: Tokyo stocks have finally managed to get off the rollercoaster they have been riding for the past few months and are gearing up for a further gradual ascent, market sources said Thursday.

After a series of big gyrations, the 225-share Nikkei average has clawed back about eight percent of its value since closing at 17,303 on January 10, its lowest finish so far this year. It is now struggling fiercely to cling to the 19,000 level.

On Thursday, Tokyo stocks were quick to recover from words of warning about excessive share rallies from U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan, helped by bargain-hunters eager to procure global blue-chip issues. The Nikkei average ended the morning session almost flat at 18,949.49.
Greenspan said caution was warranted in light of the sharp rise in the U.S. stock market during the last two years.
"The Nikkei average is basically trying to grapple for a position near the 19,000 level," said Hisao Suzuki, Yamaichi Securities deputy general manager.

Brokers said the market had already put the worst behind it. "The Nikkei average has been steadily digesting rises of 300 points or so over the weeks and although the pace is slow, it is definitely recovering," said Kenji Karikome, general manager at Daiwa Securities Co Ltd.

Karikome said that if the benchmark conquers 19,000, the next staging post would be the 19,360 level, the halfway point between the January closing low and the November 26 close of 21,418, when the first signs of weakness started to appear.
After 19,360, the 75-day moving average -- which is in the 19,500 vicinity -- would be the next technical goal, said Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd Deputy General Manager Harushige Kobayashi.

"Depending on how soon the Nikkei can cling firmly to levels above 19,000, there is a chance that it can end this fiscal year in the upper half of the 19,000 (to 20,000) band or even 20,000," Yasuo Ueki, Nikko Securities Co Ltd general manager, said.

The Nikkei's temporary comeback to the 19,000 level earlier this month came after news that the government may use state funds to buy land formerly owned by failed housing loan firms and other troubled financial institutions.
Banking, construction and real estate sectors, all sagging under the weight of bad loans, and all sectors which had been under heavy selling pressure lately were bought back.
"The utterings of politicians lifted the sectors, but in order to keep them climbing, concrete plans need to be announced," said Merrill Lynch Japan Inc strategist Keiko Kondo.
Brokers said that sharp falls seen in the past may not be repeated, unless the government decides to do something drastic like scrapping the proposed measures to solve the bad loan problem.

"There is some possibility that the market could weaken in March, as firms sell off their shareholdings ahead of their book-closings, but the Nikkei average floor is solid at the 17,303 level," Yamaichi's Kobayashi said.
Brokers said that even if the market turned sickly again, bargain-hunting of global blue chips might cushion the slide.
Turnover has been holding fairly steady at or above 400 million shares per day, a healthy volume for Tokyo, which is also a good sign, they said.

Some said the market was starting to speculate about how the economy will fare in the new fiscal year after the stifling effects of a planned sales tax hike on the economy wear off. The market has already digested the likely impact of the hike, which takes effect in April.

"The market was severely depressed late last year by the thought of the tax hike and an end to special tax cuts," Kobayashi said. "That's history now, and there do not seem to be any new, atrociously negative factors in the new year."
